src.t: USC: weight-loss drug semaglutide shows promise in reducing alcohol cravings (on a 2025 JAMA Psychiatry trial)
Substance use disorders: a comprehensive update of classification, epidemiology, neurobiology, clinical aspects, treatment and prevention

en.block: Relapse is common, and the interplay of genes, environment and trauma is poorly understood.
en.known: Addiction rewires the brain's reward circuits, and genes explain part of the risk.
en.leads: GLP-1 drugs that seem to reduce cravings, targeted brain stimulation.
en.t: Why do some people become addicted and others not?

sub.en: Why do genetic risk scores still predict who will become addicted so poorly?
Do chemical marks on DNA (epigenetics) explain lasting addiction in humans, and could they become drug targets?
Can deep brain stimulation safely help people with the most severe addictions?

src.t: van Dyck et al., Lecanemab in early Alzheimer's disease (NEJM, 2023)
Another new Alzheimer's drug: what the trial results mean (Scientific American)

en.block: The amyloid hypothesis doesn't explain everything, and damage starts years before symptoms.
en.known: Amyloid plaques and tau protein build up. Anti-amyloid antibodies slow decline somewhat.
en.leads: Neuroinflammation, a possible role for viral infections, blood biomarkers for early diagnosis.
en.t: What causes Alzheimer's disease?

sub.en: Does poor sleep help cause the build-up of tau protein, does tau disturb sleep, or both?
Why do studies disagree on whether signs of inflammation in the blood are higher in people with Alzheimer's?
How exactly does diet change the risk of developing Alzheimer's?

src.t: Global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance 1990–2021 (IHME / The Lancet)
Antimicrobial resistance crisis: could artificial intelligence be the solution?
Global shortage of innovative antibiotics fuels emergence and spread of drug-resistance

en.block: New antibiotics earn little, which has limited the interest of investors and most large drug companies.
en.known: Resistant bacteria are associated with millions of deaths a year worldwide.
en.leads: AI-discovered antibiotics such as halicin, and bacteria-killing viruses (phages).
en.t: How can we defeat antibiotic resistance?

sub.en: How can AI models that search for new antibiotics be made reliable outside test conditions and understandable rather than 'black boxes'?
How can we predict how a new drug candidate will behave inside the human body when so little data exist?
Can we predict whether a bacteria-killing virus (phage) will destroy its host right away or hide inside it?

src.t: Kirkpatrick et al., Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks (PNAS, 2017)
Three types of incremental learning

en.block: Learning new things tends to erase old ones (catastrophic forgetting).
en.known: Today's models mostly stop learning once training ends.
en.leads: External memory systems, targeted and sparse updates of the model.
en.t: Can AI keep learning from experience as humans do?

sub.en: Why is it still so hard for an AI to learn a new kind of data without forgetting what it learned before?
Can an AI keep learning without storing and replaying old examples?
How can learning a new task make an AI better at earlier tasks, instead of worse?

src.t: Müller et al., CD19 CAR T-cell therapy in autoimmune disease: a case series with follow-up (NEJM, 2024)
5 people with lupus are in remission after CAR-T cell treatment (Science News)

en.block: What triggers the attack in the first place remains unclear.
en.known: Genes and environment both play a role. CAR-T cell therapy has put some lupus patients into lasting remission.
en.leads: Resetting the immune system with CAR-T cells, vaccines that teach tolerance.
en.t: Why does the immune system attack its own body?

sub.en: Can engineered immune cells last long enough in the body to keep autoimmune disease in remission, or will repeated infusions be needed?
Which autoimmune diseases are actually suited to treatment with engineered CAR cells?
Can the serious side effects and the high cost of CAR therapy be reduced enough for wide use?

src.t: Mora et al., How many species are there on Earth and in the ocean? (PLOS Biology, 2011)

en.block: Most species, especially insects and microbes, are still unknown.
en.known: About 2 million species have been described; estimates run to many millions more.
en.leads: Environmental DNA, AI-assisted identification.
en.t: How many species live on Earth?

sub.en: How many kinds of bacteria and other microbes are there, when our counts are only a lower limit?
How can the naming of millions of unknown species be sped up, when it could take centuries at today's pace?
How many species are going extinct before we even know they exist?

src.t: The Millennium Prize Problems (Clay Mathematics Institute)

en.block: The general case is one of the Millennium Prize Problems.
en.known: The conjecture links this count to the behavior of a special function, and it is proven in some simple cases.
en.leads: Links with the Langlands program, massive computer databases of curves.
en.t: How many rational solutions does an elliptic curve have?

sub.en: Is the Tate–Shafarevich group of an elliptic curve always finite, as conjectured?
Are there general methods for finding the rational points on higher-dimensional shapes defined by equations? Almost none exist today.
Does the full conjecture hold for function fields, where Artin and Tate proved only part of it?

src.t: Good genes are nice, but joy is better (Harvard Gazette)
Friends make us happy: evidence from three European panel studies

en.block: Separating cause from correlation, and accounting for culture, is hard.
en.known: Long-running studies, one begun in 1938, find that close relationships strongly predict well-being.
en.leads: Long-term cohort studies, randomized experiments on well-being.
en.t: What makes people happy over a lifetime?

sub.en: Do friends actually make people happier, or do happier people simply find it easier to make friends?
Why do social ties seem to affect the life satisfaction of women and men differently?

src.t: Weber et al., Individualised neoantigen therapy mRNA-4157 plus pembrolizumab in resected melanoma, KEYNOTE-942 (The Lancet, 2024)
Moderna cancer vaccine results (Boston Globe, 2026)

en.block: Every tumor is diverse and evolves to resist treatment.
en.known: Immunotherapies and targeted therapies now cure some cancers that used to be fatal.
en.leads: Personalized mRNA vaccines, CAR-T cells for solid tumors, early detection from a blood test.
en.t: Can we cure most cancers?

sub.en: How can we better predict which tumor mutations a personalized vaccine should target?
How can we stop tumors from escaping a vaccine by losing its targets or hiding from the immune system?
Which biological markers can tell in advance which patients will respond to a cancer vaccine?

src.t: Direct Air Capture: executive summary (IEA)
A roadmap for achieving scalable, safe, and low-cost direct air carbon capture and storage
Potential for large-scale CO2 removal via enhanced rock weathering with croplands

en.block: It uses a lot of energy, and billions of tons per year would be needed.
en.known: Direct air capture works but still costs hundreds of dollars per ton.
en.leads: CO2 mineralization, enhanced rock weathering, new capture materials.
en.t: Can we remove CO2 from the air at scale and at low cost?

sub.en: Which capture materials can survive thousands of capture-and-release cycles in real, humid air?
How can the energy needed to capture each ton of CO2 from the air be cut sharply?
Can storing CO2 by turning it into rock underground be scaled up safely?

src.t: Team simulates a living cell that grows and divides (University of Illinois, 2026)
Bringing the genetically minimal cell to life on a computer in 4D

en.block: A human cell holds billions of interacting molecules, and the data are incomplete.
en.known: In 2026, a team simulated the complete life cycle of a minimal bacterial cell, from growth to division.
en.leads: Foundation models trained on atlases of millions of cells.
en.t: Can we simulate an entire living cell?

sub.en: How do the chromosomes of a minimal cell get shared out correctly between the two daughter cells?
What causes the strange budding and 'cell-inside-a-cell' shapes seen in the minimal cell?
How can whole-cell simulations become cheap enough in computing power to model many cells, not just a few?

src.t: Singer et al., Synchronizing volcanic, sedimentary, and ice core records of Earth's last magnetic polarity reversal (Science Advances, 2019)
Earth's magnetic field could take longer to flip than previously thought (Smithsonian)

en.block: We can't predict when the next reversal will happen.
en.known: The field has reversed hundreds of times; the last time was about 780,000 years ago.
en.leads: Simulations of the geodynamo, satellite measurements of the field.
en.t: Why does Earth's magnetic field flip?

sub.en: What triggers Earth's magnetic field to start flipping?
Is a long unstable period before the final flip typical of all magnetic reversals?
Does the weakening of today's magnetic field mean a reversal is on the way?

src.t: Global warming unlikely to be small: new study (Met Office, 2020)
IPCC AR6 Working Group I, Chapter 1
An Assessment of Earth's Climate Sensitivity Using Multiple Lines of Evidence

en.block: Clouds, too small for current models, dominate the uncertainty.
en.known: The IPCC puts the likely answer between 2.5 and 4 °C.
en.leads: Kilometer-scale climate models, AI climate emulators.
en.t: How much will Earth warm if CO2 doubles?

sub.en: Why is the way clouds respond to warming so much more uncertain than other climate feedbacks?
Why does the uneven pattern of ocean warming make past temperature records a tricky guide to future warming?
How much can past climates, such as the last ice age, narrow the range of future warming?

src.t: Mathematician proves huge result on 'dangerous' problem (Quanta, 2019)
Tao, Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values (arXiv)
Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values

en.block: Mathematics may lack the tools; it is a simple rule with no known structure to exploit.
en.known: It has been checked for enormous numbers, and in 2019 Terence Tao showed that almost all starting values get very small.
en.leads: Probabilistic methods, computer-assisted proofs.
en.t: Does the Collatz sequence always end at 1?

sub.en: Can Tao's 'almost all' result be upgraded from logarithmic density to the usual natural density?
Do almost all starting numbers drop below one fixed bound? Tao says this may be almost as hard as the full conjecture.
Could some sequence grow forever, or could there be infinitely many loops?

src.t: Sperm whale phonetic alphabet proposed for the first time (Project CETI, 2024)
Toward understanding the communication in sperm whales

en.block: Without knowing what a sound refers to, we can't translate it.
en.known: Sperm whale clicks have a combinatorial structure reminiscent of a phonetic alphabet.
en.leads: Project CETI, AI models trained on animal recordings.
en.t: Can we understand what animals say to each other?

sub.en: Do the tiny differences in the sound of each click carry information, or only the timing between clicks?
What are individual sperm whale click patterns (codas) actually used for?
What rules decide which whale 'speaks' when during an exchange?

src.t: Complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly brain (NIH, 2024)
A petavoxel fragment of human cerebral cortex reconstructed at nanoscale resolution
The burgeoning field of brain mapping

en.block: A whole human brain would mean a gigantic amount of data, on the order of a zettabyte.
en.known: The complete wiring diagram of the fruit fly brain was published in 2024. A cubic millimeter of human cortex has been mapped.
en.leads: Expansion microscopy, automatic segmentation by AI.
en.t: Can we map every connection in a human brain?

sub.en: Does the wiring seen in brain tissue removed from epilepsy patients reflect a normal brain or one changed by disease?
How much does the fine wiring of the human cortex differ from one person to another?
Why do some neurons in the deepest layer of the cortex point their branches in two opposite main directions, like a compass?

src.t: Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness (Nature, 2025)

en.block: We don't know why physical activity produces experience, and we have no objective measure of consciousness.
en.known: Brain areas and rhythms associated with conscious experience have been identified.
en.leads: Rival teams test their theories (integrated information, global workspace) together in shared experiments.
en.t: How does consciousness arise from the brain?

sub.en: Is the front of the brain (prefrontal cortex) involved in every conscious experience, or only in some?
How does the brain keep details such as an object's orientation in conscious experience while we keep looking at it?
How can results from many experiments be combined in one quantitative framework to judge rival theories of consciousness?

src.t: Richerson, Boyd and Henrich, Cultural evolution of human cooperation (2003)
The Origins and Psychology of Human Cooperation

en.block: We understand poorly why cooperation sometimes collapses.
en.known: Humans cooperate with strangers far beyond what other species do.
en.leads: Evolutionary game theory, cross-cultural experiments.
en.t: Why do humans cooperate on such a large scale?

sub.en: How did societies grow into large cooperating groups, and why did some fall apart, in different places over thousands of years?
Why are family- and clan-based institutions so much stronger in some parts of the world than in others?
How did the mental shortcuts we use to copy others' behaviour evolve, and why do they stay stable?

src.t: The Irish Citizens' Assembly (OECD Observatory of Public Sector Innovation)
‘Systematizing’ constitutional deliberation: the 2016–18 citizens’ assembly in Ireland

en.block: Polarization and the complexity of modern issues.
en.known: Citizens' assemblies, as in Ireland, have produced broadly accepted decisions on divisive issues.
en.leads: Online deliberation platforms, AI that helps groups find common ground.
en.t: Can large societies make good collective decisions on complex issues?

sub.en: How can citizens' assemblies become a lasting, normal part of how a country makes decisions, rather than one-off events?
Once a country has used citizens' assemblies, does it become easier for politicians to use them again?

src.t: No evidence that depression is caused by low serotonin levels (UCL, 2022)
The serotonin theory of depression: a systematic umbrella review of the evidence

en.block: It is probably several illnesses under one name, with no reliable biological marker.
en.known: The idea of a simple serotonin shortage is now being challenged.
en.leads: Supervised psychedelics, ketamine, targeted and personalized brain stimulation.
en.t: What really causes depression?

sub.en: How do antidepressants taken for years change the brain's serotonin system, during and after use?
What does lowering tryptophan, the building block of serotonin, really do to mood?
Can a biological marker be found that diagnoses depression or shows which treatment will work?

src.t: Vosoughi, Roy, Aral, The spread of true and false news online (Science, 2018)
The Psychological Drivers of Misinformation Belief and its Resistance to Correction

en.block: Trust in experts is often low, and false content spreads in huge volumes.
en.known: A 2018 study found that false news spread faster and further than true news on Twitter.
en.leads: Content provenance standards, community fact-checking, media literacy.
en.t: How can societies tell truth from falsehood at scale?

sub.en: Do results from small lab studies on misinformation hold up on real social media platforms at large scale?
How do people react to misinformation that is not plain written text, such as misleading images or hints rather than explicit claims?
Do corrections made as videos or cartoons work better than written corrections?

src.t: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2022: press release (Nobel Prize)
Discoveries about ancient human evolution win 2022 Nobel Prize (Scientific American)

en.block: The dates and routes of many migrations are still disputed.
en.known: Ancient DNA shows our ancestors interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans.
en.leads: Ancient DNA from bones and even from cave sediments.
en.t: How did Homo sapiens spread across the world?

sub.en: How early did groups of Homo sapiens first leave Africa, as fossils from sites in Israel and Greece suggest?
Where, when and how often did early modern humans interbreed with archaic human groups inside Africa?

src.t: FDA approves novel non-opioid treatment for moderate to severe acute pain (U.S. FDA, 2025)
The mechanisms and management of persistent postsurgical pain
Chronic Pain Among Adults — United States, 2019–2021

en.block: How the nervous system rewires itself to keep pain going is poorly understood.
en.known: Chronic pain affects roughly one adult in five in the United States. A new non-opioid painkiller was approved in the US in 2025 for acute pain.
en.leads: Painkillers targeting specific sodium channels, nerve stimulation.
en.t: Why does pain become chronic?

sub.en: Does strong pain right after surgery actually cause long-lasting pain later, or are the two only linked?
What explains the differences between women and men in how often pain persists after surgery?
Which genes make some people more likely to develop lasting pain, and can those findings be confirmed in large studies?

src.t: 1 in 4 people globally still lack access to safe drinking water (WHO/UNICEF, 2025)
Rapid groundwater decline and some cases of recovery in aquifers globally
A comprehensive review of energy consumption of seawater reverse osmosis desalination plants

en.block: Groundwater is being depleted, and desalination uses a lot of energy.
en.known: Billions of people still lack safely managed drinking water.
en.leads: Cheaper desalination membranes, water reuse, better irrigation.
en.t: Will there be enough fresh water for everyone?

sub.en: Why are groundwater levels falling faster and faster in many of the world's aquifers?
Under what conditions can a depleted aquifer recover?
Can artificially refilling aquifers, or diverting surface water, work at a large scale?

src.t: Grand prize discovery made in 2,000-year-old Herculaneum scrolls (University of Kentucky, 2024)
AI unravels ancient Roman scroll charred by volcano (Scientific American)
Advanced Techniques for the Decipherment of Ancient Scripts

en.block: Surviving texts are few and short, and the languages behind them are unknown.
en.known: The Indus script, Linear A and Rongorongo are still undeciphered. AI helped read scrolls carbonized by Vesuvius.
en.leads: Statistical and AI pattern analysis, new archaeological finds.
en.t: Can we decipher lost writing systems such as the Indus script?

sub.en: Are the Indus signs and Rongorongo real writing that records a language, or a different kind of symbol system?
How can Rongorongo be split into units of language when many of its signs look almost identical?
Can computer methods crack a truly unknown script by themselves, or can they only assist human experts?

src.t: 70% of 10-year-olds now in learning poverty (World Bank, 2022)
Experimental Evidence on Four Policies to Increase Learning at Scale

en.block: Shortages of trained teachers and materials, and teaching pitched above children's level.
en.known: In low- and middle-income countries, around 70% of ten-year-olds cannot read and understand a simple text.
en.leads: Teaching at the right level, AI tutors that work on cheap phones.
en.t: How can every child on Earth learn well?

sub.en: Can technology-based teaching tools raise learning as much as extra help from teaching assistants?
Which way of teaching children at their level gives the most learning for the money?

src.t: Findings of the BabyLM Challenge (arXiv, 2025)
The BabyLM challenge: researchers look to infants (The Transmitter)
Bridging the data gap between children and large language models

en.block: We don't know which built-in abilities let children learn so fast.
en.known: A child hears tens of millions of words; large language models train on trillions.
en.leads: Training on child-scale data, learning through interaction with the world.
en.t: Why do AIs need so much more data than children to learn?

sub.en: What built-in knowledge, if any, helps babies learn language from so few words?
How much does seeing the world and talking with people, rather than just reading text, speed up language learning?
Can a language model trained on only as many words as a child hears reach human-like language skills?

src.t: Social complexity and collapse (Complexity Science Hub, Seshat)
All Crises are Unhappy in Their Own Way: The Role of Societal Instability in Shaping the Past
When Collapse Wasn't Inevitable: How Some Societies Turned Crisis into Renewal

en.block: There are few cases, each different, so general laws are hard to test.
en.known: Studies of past crises point to pressures such as widespread impoverishment, more people competing for elite positions than there are places, and strained state finances.
en.leads: Large historical databases such as Seshat, quantitative history.
en.t: Why do civilizations collapse?

sub.en: Why do some societal crises end in collapse while others lead to reform and renewal?
Why do the different consequences of a societal crisis not tend to happen together?

src.t: DESI results suggest dark energy may evolve over time (UKRI)
DESI DR2 results. II. Measurements of baryon acoustic oscillations and cosmological constraints
TASI Lectures on the Cosmological Constant

en.block: Quantum physics predicts a value some 60 to 120 orders of magnitude larger than observations allow. This is a serious crisis in physics.
en.known: The expansion of the universe is accelerating. The cause, called dark energy, makes up about 70% of its energy content.
en.leads: DESI surveys hint that it may change over time; Euclid and the Rubin Observatory will measure it more precisely.
en.t: What is dark energy?

sub.en: Does dark energy really change over time, as DESI's 2025 data suggest?
Could an unknown error in the measurements, rather than new physics, explain this hint?
Why do galaxy maps and the cosmic microwave background give slightly different values for the universe's parameters?

src.t: Thermodynamic Asymmetry in Time (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

en.block: No one knows why the universe began in such an improbable, low-entropy state.
en.known: Entropy, or disorder, always increases, and this is tied to the very ordered state of the early universe.
en.leads: Cosmology of the Big Bang, quantum thermodynamics.
en.t: Why does time flow in only one direction?

sub.en: Does the very low entropy of the early universe (the 'Past Hypothesis') itself need an explanation?
Do the other arrows of time, such as memory or cause and effect, come down to the growth of entropy?
How can we justify the probability rule physicists use to explain why systems move toward equilibrium?

src.t: Achievement of target gain larger than unity in an inertial fusion experiment (Phys. Rev. Lett. 2024)
US Department of Energy details net energy gain (Photonics)

en.block: Net gain for the whole plant, materials that survive, and tritium supply are still unsolved.
en.known: In 2022, the US National Ignition Facility got more fusion energy out than the laser energy sent onto the target.
en.leads: ITER, compact tokamaks with high-temperature superconducting magnets, and dozens of private startups.
en.t: Can nuclear fusion produce electricity economically?

sub.en: Which materials can survive years of bombardment by the 14 MeV neutrons produced by fusion?
Can a power plant breed enough tritium from lithium to fuel itself?
Which materials can withstand the divertor, the part of the reactor that faces the harshest conditions?

src.t: ENCODE Project Consortium, An integrated encyclopedia of DNA elements in the human genome (Nature, 2012)
Hidden treasures in junk DNA (Scientific American)

en.block: How much of the rest has a function is still hotly debated.
en.known: Only about 1–2% of the human genome codes for proteins.
en.leads: Large-scale functional screens, AI models trained on whole genomes.
en.t: What does most of our DNA actually do?

sub.en: Does a stretch of DNA being copied into RNA mean it has a real function?
How can we tell a useful non-coding RNA apart from one that does nothing?
How many non-coding RNAs with a real job are still waiting to be found?

src.t: Oliveira e Silva, Herzog, Pardi, Empirical verification of the even Goldbach conjecture and computation of prime gaps up to 4·10^18 (Mathematics of Computation, 2014)

en.block: No proof for all even numbers, despite almost three centuries of effort.
en.known: Checked by computer up to 4 × 10^18. A weaker version for odd numbers was proven in 2013.
en.leads: Analytic number theory and sieve methods.
en.t: Is every even number greater than 2 the sum of two primes?

sub.en: Are the Hardy–Littlewood predictions for how many ways numbers split into two primes, and for prime gaps, actually correct?

src.t: Quantum Gravity (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
A tabletop experiment for quantum gravity (AIP Inside Science)

en.block: They are incompatible, and no experiment reaches the Planck scale where their conflict would show.
en.known: General relativity and quantum mechanics each work perfectly in their own domain.
en.leads: String theory, loop quantum gravity, lab tests of entanglement through gravity.
en.t: How can gravity and quantum mechanics be unified?

sub.en: How can time be described when spacetime itself is quantum (the 'problem of time')?
Must gravity be quantized at all?
Does loop quantum gravity give back Einstein's general relativity at low energies?

src.t: Fearon, Rationalist explanations for war (International Organization, 1995)

en.block: Each conflict is unique, and predicting them is very hard.
en.known: Most rivalries never become wars; wars often come from failed bargaining and mistrust.
en.leads: Early-warning models, research on mediation and deterrence.
en.t: Why do wars start, and how can they be prevented?

sub.en: Why does a breakdown in bargaining sometimes lead to war, and other times to protests, coups or no violence at all?
How can researchers tell whether a given war came from hidden information or from promises that could not be trusted?
Can the same theory that explains why wars start also explain how lasting peace is kept?

src.t: Riess et al., JWST observations reject unrecognized crowding of Cepheid photometry as an explanation for the Hubble tension (Astrophysical Journal Letters, 2024)
JWST complicates expanding universe paradox by checking Hubble's work (Space.com)

en.block: Neither side has found an error that would explain the gap.
en.known: Measurements from the nearby universe give an expansion rate near 73 km/s/Mpc; those from the early universe give about 67.
en.leads: Independent distance checks with the James Webb telescope, possible new physics in the early universe.
en.t: Why do measurements of the universe's expansion rate disagree?

sub.en: Is the gap caused by new physics, by unexpected large-scale structures, or by several unrelated errors?
Could early or evolving dark energy, or new interactions of neutrinos, resolve the tension?

src.t: Butlin, Long et al., Consciousness in artificial intelligence: insights from the science of consciousness (arXiv)
Identifying indicators of consciousness in AI systems

en.block: The answer depends on the unsolved question of human consciousness.
en.known: There is no recognized method to test consciousness in an artificial system.
en.leads: Indicator checklists drawn from scientific theories of consciousness.
en.t: Can an AI be conscious?

sub.en: Is consciousness only a matter of performing the right computations, whatever the material the system is made of?
Why can't we just test an AI's behavior to find out if it is conscious, when it may be trained to imitate humans?
How can we avoid believing that AI systems are conscious when they only seem to be?

src.t: Brynjolfsson, Li, Raymond, Generative AI at Work (NBER)
Generative AI at Work

en.block: Most studies cover a few tasks or companies; the effects on the whole economy are not yet known.
en.known: Early studies show large productivity gains on some tasks.
en.leads: Measuring how AI is actually used at work, policies for transitions.
en.t: How will AI change work and the economy?

sub.en: Why do newer, less-skilled workers gain the most from AI assistants, while experts gain little?
Do workers who use AI assistants actually learn skills they keep?
Why does AI change productivity so differently from one worker to another?

src.t: Energy and AI: executive summary (International Energy Agency, 2025)
Electricity Demand and Grid Impacts of AI Data Centers: Challenges and Prospects

en.block: Grids and clean power plants take years to build.
en.known: Electricity demand from data centers is growing fast.
en.leads: More efficient chips, nuclear power contracts, placing data centers near clean energy.
en.t: How can AI's energy needs be met sustainably?

sub.en: How can the power use of AI data centers be forecast accurately when it can change so fast?
Can AI computing jobs be shifted in time or place to match when and where clean power is available?
How can sudden swings in a data center's power use be kept from destabilizing the electricity grid?

src.t: International AI Safety Report 2025 (UK Government)
Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

en.block: We can't yet verify what a model is really trying to do, or guarantee its behavior.
en.known: Current models are highly capable and improving fast.
en.leads: Interpretability, scalable oversight, evaluations of dangerous capabilities.
en.t: How do we build general AI that is reliable and aligned with our interests?

sub.en: How can people check an AI's work on tasks that are too hard for them to judge?
How can we stop an AI from exploiting flaws in the reward it is trained to maximize?
Why can an AI behave badly once in use, even if it was rewarded correctly during training?

src.t: Towards Guaranteed Safe AI: a framework for robust and reliable AI systems (arXiv, 2024)
Algorithms for Verifying Deep Neural Networks

en.block: Neural networks are far too large and opaque for current proof methods.
en.known: Formal verification already proves the correctness of some critical software.
en.leads: Verifying small parts or outputs, AI that writes its own checkable proofs.
en.t: Can we mathematically prove that an AI system is safe?

sub.en: How can a vague idea like 'harm' be turned into a precise rule that a computer can check?
Can we build models of the world accurate enough to prove what an AI's actions will cause?
Can AI systems be trained to write the safety proofs that are now too much work for human experts?

src.t: Kalai et al., Why language models hallucinate (arXiv, 2025)
A Survey on Hallucination in Large Language Models: Principles, Taxonomy, Challenges, and Open Questions

en.block: They still state false things confidently and misjudge their own uncertainty.
en.known: Reasoning models have improved sharply on mathematics and code.
en.leads: Automatic verification of answers, training on checked results, calibrated confidence.
en.t: Can AI reason reliably and know when it is wrong?

sub.en: How can an AI learn to recognize the limits of its own knowledge?
Would AIs make up fewer false answers if tests stopped rewarding guessing over saying 'I don't know'?
Why can extra training make a model worse at judging how confident it should be?

src.t: Stokes et al., A deep learning approach to antibiotic discovery (Cell, 2020)
Autoscience builds automated research lab (SiliconANGLE, 2026)

en.block: Coming up with truly new questions and checking results remain hard.
en.known: AI has helped predict protein structures and discover materials and antibiotics, and companies are building automated labs.
en.leads: Self-driving labs, AI agents that design and run experiments.
en.t: Can AI systems carry out scientific research on their own?

sub.en: How can scientists tell when an AI tool's results can't be trusted?
Can an AI system build real scientific understanding on its own?

src.t: Huang et al., Collective Constitutional AI: aligning a language model with public input (arXiv, 2024)
Collective Constitutional AI: aligning a language model with public input (Anthropic)
Position: Social Choice Should Guide AI Alignment in Dealing with Diverse Human Feedback

en.block: People and cultures disagree, and there is no accepted way to combine their views.
en.known: Models are trained with written principles and human feedback.
en.leads: Public input processes, published constitutions for AI models.
en.t: Whose values should AI follow?

sub.en: How can conflicting views from many people be combined into consistent rules for how an AI should behave?
Can the science of voting and group decisions (social choice) tell us how to choose an AI's values?

src.t: World Inequality Report 2018: executive summary
Global Income Inequality, 1820–2020: the Persistence and Mutation of Extreme Inequality

en.block: Technology, trade, taxes and politics are tangled together.
en.known: Inequality between countries has fallen in recent decades, while within many countries it has risen.
en.leads: Better tax and income data, natural experiments.
en.t: What makes inequality rise or fall?

sub.en: How can we measure the incomes of the very richest people accurately when household surveys miss them?
Could new rules, such as countries sharing tax revenue, substantially reduce inequality across the world?

src.t: What makes us human? Comparing brain development in humans and great apes (TU Dresden, 2026)
Genetics of human brain development

en.block: We don't know which differences actually matter.
en.known: Humans have many neurons in the cortex and a long childhood.
en.leads: Comparing human and ape brain organoids.
en.t: What makes human intelligence different from other animals'?

sub.en: Which human-specific genes and DNA regions made our cortex grow larger, beyond the handful studied so far?
Do genetic changes that alter the brain's physical structure actually change complex abilities such as thinking and behavior?

src.t: An accurate and rapidly calibrating speech neuroprosthesis (NEJM, 2024)
The state of clinical trials of implantable brain–computer interfaces

en.block: Long-term implant safety and the amount of information that can be read remain limited.
en.known: Implants have let paralyzed people move a cursor and produce speech from their brain signals.
en.leads: High-density electrodes, less invasive designs.
en.t: Can brain–computer interfaces restore lost abilities?

sub.en: Can electrodes implanted in the brain keep working reliably for a person's whole life?
How few brain signals are actually enough to control a device accurately?
How can brain implant trials include a fair range of people, since women have been underrepresented so far?

src.t: Cunningham et al., Sparse autoencoders find highly interpretable features in language models (arXiv, 2023)
Open-sourcing circuit tracing tools (Anthropic)
Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability

en.block: Models are huge, and each neuron mixes several concepts.
en.known: We can isolate internal concepts and circuits in large language models.
en.leads: Feature dictionaries, circuit tracing, automated analysis tools.
en.t: Can we understand what happens inside a neural network?

sub.en: What exactly counts as a 'feature', or concept, inside a neural network?
How can we check that an explanation of what a network is doing is actually correct?
Can the work of understanding AI models be automated and kept affordable as models keep growing?

src.t: Hauser et al., The mystery of language evolution (Frontiers in Psychology, 2014)

en.block: Language leaves no fossils.
en.known: Several of the abilities it needs exist in other animals, but none combines them all.
en.leads: Comparative genetics, animal communication studies, models of how languages evolve.
en.t: How did human language emerge?

sub.en: When did the brain machinery for grammar and meaning appear in our ancestors?
How do specific genes lead to the ability to use language?
Does any animal communication system have anything like the grammar of human language?

src.t: Gaitsgory and Raskin, Proof of the geometric Langlands conjecture I: construction of the functor (arXiv, 2024; first of a series of papers)
Monumental proof settles geometric Langlands conjecture (Quanta, 2024)
Langlands Program, trace formulas, and their geometrization

en.block: The arithmetic version, closest to prime numbers, remains largely open.
en.known: It is a vast web of conjectures linking number theory, geometry and symmetry. The geometric version was proven in 2024.
en.leads: Extending the methods of the geometric proof.
en.t: Is the Langlands program true?

sub.en: Can Langlands's principle of functoriality be proved in general?
Can trace formulas be used to prove functoriality, as Frenkel, Langlands and Ngô propose?
Can the link between elliptic curves and modular forms, used to prove Fermat's Last Theorem, be extended to its general form?

src.t: Libet and free will revisited (Discover)
Free Will (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

en.block: What these experiments show is disputed, and the concept itself is debated.
en.known: Brain activity can be measured before a person reports deciding to act.
en.leads: Neuroscience of decision-making, joint work between philosophers and neuroscientists.
en.t: Do we have free will?

sub.en: Does the brain signal recorded before a movement (the 'readiness potential') reflect a decision, or just random background brain activity?
Does this signal mark the start of an action, or something more general such as expecting or paying attention?
Why do some people show no readiness potential at all?

src.t: Olympiad-level formal mathematical reasoning with reinforcement learning (Nature, 2025)
Google DeepMind achieves gold-level Math Olympiad performance, matching OpenAI (TechRepublic, 2025)

en.block: Research needs new concepts, not just solving problems someone else posed.
en.known: In 2025, AI systems reached gold-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad.
en.leads: Formal proofs in the Lean proof assistant, collaboration between mathematicians and AI.
en.t: Can AI discover major mathematical results on its own?

sub.en: Can AI reliably translate ordinary mathematical writing into formal, machine-checkable statements (autoformalization)?
Can AI propose new conjectures and concepts, not just solve problems written by humans?
How can AI learn formal mathematics when so few human-written formal proofs exist to train on?

src.t: Optimisation of the Search for CP-symmetry Violation at the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment
Constraint on the matter–antimatter symmetry-violating phase in neutrino oscillations

en.block: The known asymmetries between them are far too weak to explain our existence.
en.known: The Big Bang should have produced equal amounts of matter and antimatter, which would have annihilated.
en.leads: Neutrino oscillations (DUNE, Hyper-Kamiokande) and measurements of the electric dipole moment.
en.t: Why is there more matter than antimatter?

sub.en: Do neutrinos and antineutrinos oscillate differently, which would mean CP violation among leptons?
Could CP violation among leptons have created the excess of matter, through a process called leptogenesis?

src.t: LZ experiment sees surprising result in search for dark matter (2026)
LZ experiment sets new record in search for dark matter
A new era in the search for dark matter

en.block: Decades of direct-detection experiments have confirmed nothing; in 2026 LZ reported one candidate event, far below the threshold for a discovery.
en.known: About 85% of the matter in the universe is invisible. We detect it only through its gravitational pull on galaxies and light.
en.leads: Massive particles (WIMPs), axions, next-generation underground detectors, or a modification of gravity.
en.t: What is dark matter?

sub.en: If dark matter is made of WIMPs, could they be lighter or give weaker signals than the simplest models predict?
Do puzzles in small galaxies (such as cusp-core and missing satellites) point to dark matter that interacts with itself, or to errors in simulations?
Could gravitational waves from black holes reveal dark matter gathered around them?

src.t: Tonegawa, Morrissey, Kitamura, The role of engram cells in the systems consolidation of memory (Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2018)

en.block: We can't read a memory from a brain, or explain how it stays stable for decades.
en.known: In mice, groups of neurons carrying a specific memory have been identified.
en.leads: Mapping neural connections, imaging individual synapses.
en.t: How are memories stored?

sub.en: How do signals from the hippocampus switch on 'silent' memory cells in the cortex?
How do memory cells in the hippocampus fall silent over time, and is this passive fading or an active process?
Does the cortex use separate groups of cells for memories of events and for memories of facts?

src.t: Measurement in Quantum Theory (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

en.block: Rival interpretations (many worlds, wave-function collapse and others) make the same predictions, so experiments can't easily separate them.
en.known: Quantum mechanics predicts the probabilities of results with extraordinary precision.
en.leads: Tests of objective collapse using ever larger objects in quantum superposition.
en.t: What really happens when a quantum system is measured?

sub.en: At what size does the quantum world give way to the classical world we see?
Can interference experiments with ever larger molecules or tiny levitated objects confirm or rule out collapse models?
Does gravity cause the wave function to collapse, as Diósi and Penrose proposed?

src.t: Papenburg et al., Causal role of the gut microbiome in certain human diseases: a narrative review (eGastroenterology, 2024)

en.block: Most links are correlations; proving cause is hard.
en.known: Gut bacteria are linked to obesity, immunity and perhaps mood.
en.leads: Controlled trials of fecal transplants, targeted therapeutic bacteria.
en.t: What exact role does the microbiome play in our health?

sub.en: How exactly does the microbiome influence health and disease?
Which measurements of the microbiome are reliable enough to predict a person's health?
Can fecal transplants and living bacterial treatments be made safe and available on a large scale?

src.t: Awad et al., The Moral Machine experiment (Nature, 2018)
Do infants have a sense of fairness?
Seven Moral Rules Found All Around the World

en.block: Separating what is innate from what is cultural is hard.
en.known: Some moral intuitions, such as fairness, appear across cultures and even in infants.
en.leads: Large cross-cultural surveys, studies with young children.
en.t: Where do our moral values come from?

sub.en: Why do societies rank the same moral values differently, for example putting family above the wider group or the reverse?
How are a society's moral values linked to its size, how much people move around, and how unequal it is?
Can moral rules about sex, religion and politics also be explained as ways of helping people cooperate?

src.t: Improving the matrix multiplication exponent with modern optimization and AlphaEvolve (arXiv, 2026)
Fast matrix multiplication: Limitations of the Coppersmith-Winograd method

en.block: No one knows whether the ideal exponent of 2 is reachable.
en.known: The best known exponent is about 2.371; in 2026, an AI-assisted search lowered it slightly once more.
en.leads: Algebraic methods, AI-driven algorithm search.
en.t: How fast can two matrices be multiplied?

sub.en: Is the matrix multiplication exponent equal to 2, so that two n×n matrices can be multiplied in about n^(2+ε) steps for any ε > 0?
Can a new method get past the proven limits of the 'laser method', whose wide family of variants cannot go below an exponent of 2.3078?
How fast can rectangular (non-square) matrices of different shapes be multiplied?

src.t: Global population to peak this century: World Population Prospects 2024 (IISD)
Fertility in High-Income Countries: Trends, Patterns, Determinants, and Consequences
Policy responses to low fertility: How effective are they?

en.block: Family policies can raise births for a while, but their long-term effect on fertility is often limited.
en.known: More than half of the world's countries now have fertility below replacement level.
en.leads: Studies of housing costs, work and family life, and changing norms.
en.t: Why are birth rates falling almost everywhere?

sub.en: When people say how many children they want, is that a general ideal or a real plan for their own lives?

src.t: The Millennium Prize Problems (Clay Mathematics Institute)

en.block: We can't prove they never blow up to infinite values, and turbulence remains poorly understood.
en.known: These equations describe water, air and weather, and are used everywhere in engineering.
en.leads: AI-assisted search for singularities and computer-verified proofs.
en.t: Do the equations of fluids always have a smooth solution?

sub.en: For any large starting flow in three dimensions, do smooth solutions exist forever, or can they blow up?
Are Leray's weak solutions unique?
Can the Caffarelli–Kohn–Nirenberg theorem, which limits the size of possible singularities, be improved?

src.t: Davies et al., Loihi: a neuromorphic manycore processor with on-chip learning (IEEE Micro, 2018)
Intel unveils largest-ever neuromorphic computer, Hala Point (Live Science, 2024)
Brain-inspired computing – We need a master plan

en.block: Today's chips separate memory and computation, which wastes energy.
en.known: The human brain runs on about 20 watts.
en.leads: Neuromorphic chips, analog and optical computing.
en.t: Can computers become as energy-efficient as the brain?

sub.en: How can brain-like chips learn using only the information available locally at each connection?
For which tasks do neuromorphic chips really use much less energy than ordinary processors?

src.t: New KATRIN results (KIT)
Direct neutrino-mass measurement based on 259 days of KATRIN data (Science, 2025)

en.block: We don't know their exact mass or whether they are their own antiparticle.
en.known: Neutrinos have a tiny mass, while the Standard Model predicted zero.
en.leads: KATRIN measures the mass; neutrinoless double beta decay experiments chase the second question.
en.t: Where does the mass of neutrinos come from?

sub.en: What exactly is the neutrino mass? In 2025 KATRIN set an upper limit of 0.45 eV.
Are neutrinos their own antiparticles (Majorana particles)? Neutrinoless double-beta decay would prove it.
How can nuclear theory link a measured double-beta decay rate to the new physics behind it?

src.t: Business-as-usual not an option with future global food security in jeopardy (UN News, FAO)
Biological nitrogen fixation and prospects for ecological intensification in cereal-based cropping systems

en.block: Yields must rise further on less land, water and fertilizer.
en.known: Crop yields have risen sharply over decades, but farming drives deforestation and emissions.
en.leads: Cereals that fix their own nitrogen, farming that needs less fertilizer.
en.t: Can we feed 10 billion people without destroying ecosystems?

sub.en: Can cereals like wheat, rice and maize be engineered to fix their own nitrogen from the air?
How much nitrogen can free-living soil bacteria provide to cereal crops?
How can crops' need for nitrogen, expected to at least double by 2050, be met without more fertilizer pollution?

src.t: USC study confirms the rotation of Earth's inner core has slowed (USC, 2024)
Inner core backtracking by seismic waveform change reversals

en.block: Only seismic waves can probe it, indirectly.
en.known: A solid iron-nickel inner core sits inside a liquid outer core, and its rotation appears to vary over time.
en.leads: Denser seismometer networks, lab experiments at extreme pressures.
en.t: What exactly is at the center of the Earth?

sub.en: What makes the inner core speed up and then slow down relative to the rest of the planet?
Why did the inner core move back along its path more slowly than it moved forward?
How do the solid inner core, the liquid outer core and the mantle pull on one another?

src.t: Once-weekly semaglutide in adults with overweight or obesity (NEJM, 2021)

en.block: Their full action in the brain and their very long-term effects are not well understood.
en.known: GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide produce large, lasting weight loss.
en.leads: Drugs combining several gut hormones, studies of their effects on addiction and heart disease.
en.t: How does the body regulate weight, and why do GLP-1 drugs work so well?

sub.en: Which brain circuits are responsible for the weight loss caused by GLP-1 drugs?
Why do about 10–15% of people on semaglutide lose little or no weight?

src.t: Ocean Census reveals more than 1,100 new species (Scientific American)
Bell et al., study of how much of the deep seafloor has been visually observed (Science Advances, 2025): repository record
How little we've seen: A visual coverage estimate of the deep seafloor

en.block: Reaching the depths is slow and expensive.
en.known: Most of the deep seafloor has never been explored, and expeditions keep finding new species.
en.leads: Autonomous underwater robots, environmental DNA collected from seawater.
en.t: What lives in the deep ocean?

sub.en: Which deep-sea places should be explored next to fill the biggest gaps in what we have seen?
Can cheaper, autonomous robots make deep-sea exploration fast enough to see much more of the seafloor?
How much does our picture of deep-sea life reflect only the few places, like canyons near rich countries, that have been studied most?

src.t: Google Quantum AI, Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold (Nature, 2024)
Meet Willow, our state-of-the-art quantum chip (Google)

en.block: It will likely take hundreds of thousands to millions of reliable physical qubits.
en.known: Logical qubits protected by error correction have been demonstrated in the lab.
en.leads: Surface codes, neutral atoms, trapped ions, topological qubits.
en.t: Can we build a useful, fault-tolerant quantum computer?

sub.en: What causes the rare bursts of correlated errors, seen about once an hour, and how can they be stopped?
Can error-correction decoding keep up in real time as quantum processors grow larger?
How can 'leakage', when qubits escape their two working states, be controlled?

src.t: MGH performs second xenotransplant of gene-edited pig kidney into living recipient (Mass General Brigham, 2025)
Gene-edited pig kidney transplanted into third person (STAT, 2024)
2025: status of cardiac xenotransplantation including preclinical models

en.block: Rejection and long-term survival of these organs remain major hurdles.
en.known: Since 2022, gene-edited pig hearts and kidneys have been transplanted into living patients.
en.leads: Further gene-edited pigs, 3D bioprinting, organs grown from a patient's own cells.
en.t: Can we produce organs for transplant on demand?

sub.en: How can doctors detect rejection of a pig organ early, when most anti-pig antibodies stick to the organ itself instead of circulating in the blood?
Which combination of immune-suppressing drugs can keep a pig organ working in a person for years?
How does a pig organ's own growth affect how well it works inside a human body?

src.t: LiteBIRD Collaboration (Campeti et al.), LiteBIRD science goals and forecasts: origin of primordial gravitational waves (arXiv, 2023)
Planck 2018 results: X. Constraints on inflation

en.block: Known physics breaks down at time zero, and inflation is not yet confirmed.
en.known: The observable universe is 13.8 billion years old; a very brief phase of inflation is likely.
en.leads: Searching for primordial gravitational waves in the cosmic microwave background (LiteBIRD, Simons Observatory).
en.t: What happened at the very beginning of the universe?

sub.en: Did inflation produce primordial gravitational waves? Their strength (the ratio r) is now limited to below 0.056.
What shape was the energy landscape (the potential) that drove inflation? Data increasingly favour concave shapes.
Did inflation involve anything beyond the simplest 'slow-roll' behaviour? No evidence has been found so far.

src.t: Harrison et al., Life as a guide to its own origins (Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics, 2023)
The ocean vents where life on Earth likely began (JSTOR Daily)

en.block: No complete chemical pathway explains the step from simple molecules to a first cell.
en.known: Life has existed on Earth for at least 3.5 billion years.
en.leads: The RNA world, hydrothermal vents, prebiotic chemistry and directed evolution in the lab.
en.t: How did life begin?

sub.en: How could the purine building blocks of RNA (such as A and G) form without enzymes?
Can RNA strands link up into chains inside watery, cell-like bubbles (protocells)?
What were the membranes of the last universal common ancestor of all life (LUCA) made of?

src.t: The Millennium Prize Problems (Clay Mathematics Institute)

en.block: Several major families of proof techniques have been proven insufficient.
en.known: Posed in 1971: if a problem is easy to check, is it also easy to solve?
en.leads: Geometric complexity theory, circuit lower bounds.
en.t: Is P equal to NP?

sub.en: Can anyone prove that some explicitly given problem needs Boolean circuits of more than linear size? The best known lower bound is only about 4n.
Is NP different from co-NP? Equivalently, is there no proof system with short proofs of every tautology?
Which proof techniques can get past the known barriers of 'relativization' and 'natural proofs'?

src.t: Malaria fact sheet (World Health Organization)
Driving down malaria transmission with engineered gene drives
Antibody reduces risk of malaria in children

en.block: Parasites resist drugs and mosquitoes resist insecticides.
en.known: The WHO now recommends two malaria vaccines, yet the disease still kills hundreds of thousands a year, mostly young children in Africa.
en.leads: Gene drives to suppress mosquito populations, long-acting monoclonal antibodies.
en.t: Can malaria be eradicated?

sub.en: How can mosquitoes be prevented from evolving resistance to a gene drive?
Will gene drives work in the wild, when none has yet been tested in the open environment?
Can a gene drive spread through and suppress whole wild mosquito populations, especially where seasons change sharply?

src.t: The 100 Days Mission (CEPI)
Brief on wastewater surveillance (Brown University Pandemic Center, 2025)
100-Day Mission for Future Pandemic Vaccines, Viewed Through the Lens of Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs)

en.block: Detecting new outbreaks is slow and very unequal across the world.
en.known: In 2020, mRNA vaccines were designed within days of the virus's genome being published.
en.leads: Wastewater surveillance, vaccines prepared in advance for whole virus families.
en.t: Can we stop the next pandemic before it spreads?

sub.en: Can a vaccine really be developed and delivered within 100 days of a new virus being reported?
How can poorer countries be included from the start, so that faster vaccines do not widen existing inequalities?
Can wastewater testing, which tracked COVID-19 trends, be extended to catch other dangerous viruses and their variants early?

src.t: Poverty and Inequality Update, Fall 2025 (World Bank)
General equilibrium effects of cash transfers: experimental evidence from Kenya

en.block: The remaining poverty is concentrated in fragile and conflict-hit countries.
en.known: The number of people in extreme poverty fell from about 2.3 billion in 1990 to about 831 million in 2025, about one person in ten.
en.leads: Direct cash transfers, growth, better data on who is poor.
en.t: Can extreme poverty be ended?

sub.en: Are there poverty traps that only a large enough sum of money can break, and how big would that sum be for different families?
Do the benefits of cash transfers last more than four years after the money is received?

src.t: Scientists engineer shortcut for photosynthetic glitch (University of Illinois, Science 2019)
Synthetic glycolate metabolism pathways stimulate crop growth and productivity in the field

en.block: The key enzyme, Rubisco, is slow and often grabs oxygen by mistake.
en.known: Crops turn only a small percentage of sunlight into biomass. Engineered plants with a bypass for wasteful reactions grew much more in field trials.
en.leads: Engineering metabolic bypasses, improved Rubisco, artificial photosynthesis.
en.t: Can photosynthesis be made more efficient?

sub.en: Will the extra growth from a photorespiration bypass turn into more grain, seeds or tubers in food crops?
Does the engineered bypass really work inside plant cells the way scientists designed it?
How much can fixing this wasteful reaction help crops in hot, dry climates, where the losses are greatest?

src.t: Global Tipping Points Report 2025 reveals first Earth system tipping point reached (NOC)
Earth system tipping point risks (Global Tipping Points Report)
Exceeding 1.5°C global warming could trigger multiple climate tipping points

en.block: The exact thresholds are uncertain, and we may find them too late.
en.known: Fragile systems have been identified: Atlantic currents, ice sheets, the Amazon. In 2025, scientists concluded that warm-water coral reefs have already crossed theirs.
en.leads: Early-warning signals in observational data.
en.t: Where are the climate's tipping points?

sub.en: At what level of warming does each tipping system, such as an ice sheet or the Amazon, actually tip?
Can we build reliable early warnings that a tipping point is getting close?
Which tipping points could already be triggered at today's level of warming?

src.t: The bounded gaps between primes Polymath project: a retrospective (arXiv)
Stadlmann, Bounded gaps between primes (arXiv, 2026)
Variants of the Selberg sieve, and bounded intervals containing many primes

en.block: Bringing the gap down to 2 seems to need fundamentally new ideas.
en.known: Since 2013 we know there are infinitely many pairs of primes separated by a bounded gap; the bound was 246, and a 2026 preprint lowers it to 240.
en.leads: Refinements of sieve methods.
en.t: Are there infinitely many twin primes?

sub.en: Can the 'parity problem' be overcome? Sieve methods alone cannot push the gap below 6.
Is the generalized Elliott–Halberstam conjecture, about how evenly primes are spread out, true? It would bring the bound down to 6.
How short can an interval be and still contain three or more primes infinitely often?

src.t: Price et al., Probabilistic weather forecasting with machine learning (Nature, 2024)
GenCast predicts weather and the risks of extreme conditions (Google DeepMind, Nature 2024)
What Is the Predictability Limit of Midlatitude Weather?

en.block: The chaos of the atmosphere seems to limit forecasts to around two weeks.
en.known: AI models now match or beat the best traditional forecasts up to about 15 days ahead.
en.leads: AI ensemble forecasts, monthly and seasonal predictions.
en.t: How far ahead can weather be predicted?

sub.en: Can AI weather models ever work without the traditional physics-based models that supply their training data and starting conditions?
How can forecasts best describe the uncertainty that grows quickly beyond a few days ahead?

src.t: Bloom, Jones, Van Reenen, Webb, Are ideas getting harder to find? (NBER)
Are Ideas Getting Harder to Find?

en.block: Measurement problems and the possibility that new ideas are getting harder to find.
en.known: Productivity growth in rich countries has been weaker since the mid-2000s.
en.leads: AI as a general-purpose technology, reforms that speed up building and research.
en.t: Why has productivity growth slowed in rich countries?

sub.en: Why does each new idea now take more researchers: do teams duplicate each other's work, or do discoveries spill over less than before?
Are patents a reliable way to count new ideas when what can be patented has changed over the decades?

src.t: De novo design of protein structure and function with RFdiffusion (Nature, 2023)
Jumper et al., Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold (Nature, 2021)

en.block: Shape isn't everything: motion, interactions and function remain hard to predict.
en.known: AlphaFold predicts the shape of almost every known protein.
en.leads: Generative models that design proteins from scratch, custom enzymes and drugs.
en.t: Can we predict what any protein does, and design new ones at will?

sub.en: How can design programs handle the small molecules that proteins must grab hold of, such as a drug or a substrate?
Can designed proteins be made to stick only to their intended target and to nothing else in the body?
Why do design methods still fail on the hardest tasks, and why do many designs not work when actually made in the lab?

src.t: Molecular basis of positional memory in limb regeneration (Nature, 2025)
New insight into regeneration in mammals (ScienceDaily)

en.block: We don't know what switches regeneration off in mammals.
en.known: Salamanders regrow whole limbs; the human liver can partly regrow itself.
en.leads: Organoids, bioelectric signals that guide tissue shape, gene regulation studies in regenerating animals.
en.t: Can humans regrow lost limbs and organs?

sub.en: What gives the cells of a regenerating limb the ability to change their memory of where they are in the body?

src.t: Konkoly et al., Real-time dialogue between experimenters and dreamers during REM sleep (Current Biology, 2021)

en.block: There is no agreed function for dreaming.
en.known: Vivid dreams occur mostly during REM sleep.
en.leads: Memory replay, rehearsal of threats, lucid dreamers who can signal from inside a dream.
en.t: What are dreams for?

sub.en: Does dreaming bring any benefit to how the brain works?
Is two-way communication with a sleeping person possible only during lucid dreams, or also in ordinary ones?

src.t: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson awarded 2024 Nobel Prize (NBER)
The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development: An Empirical Investigation

en.block: We can't run experiments on whole countries.
en.known: Institutions matter a lot, as the 2024 Nobel Prize in economics recognized.
en.leads: Natural experiments, satellite data on night-time lights, small-scale controlled trials.
en.t: Why do some nations become rich and others not?

sub.en: How solid is the evidence linking the death rates of early colonial settlers to the quality of a country's institutions today?

src.t: The Millennium Prize Problems (Clay Mathematics Institute)
The Riemann hypothesis is true up to 3·10^12

en.block: No approach has succeeded since 1859.
en.known: Checked by computer for trillions of cases. It governs how prime numbers are distributed.
en.leads: Links with random-matrix physics, computer-verified formal proofs.
en.t: Is the Riemann hypothesis true?

sub.en: More than 40% of the zeros are known to lie on the critical line. Can this be raised to 100%?
Does the Riemann hypothesis hold for even one of the related 'L-functions'? Not a single case is known.
Do the spacings between zeros really follow the Dyson–Montgomery conjectures, which computer calculations strongly support?

src.t: Why humanoid robots aren't advancing as fast as AI chatbots (The Robot Report)
Are we truly on the verge of a humanoid robot revolution? (UC Berkeley)
Foundation models in robotics: Applications, challenges, and the future

en.block: There is little data on physical skills compared with text.
en.known: Robots excel in factories but struggle in messy places like homes; what is easy for us is often hard for them.
en.leads: Robot foundation models, training in simulation, humanoid robots.
en.t: Can robots handle the physical world as well as we do?

sub.en: Where can robots get enough training data about physical tasks, when there is so little compared with text?
How can we guarantee that a robot run by a large AI model acts safely and knows when it is unsure?
Can large AI models run fast enough to control a robot in real time?

src.t: FDA approves drug with new mechanism of action for treatment of schizophrenia (U.S. FDA, 2024)
Rethinking the First Episode of Schizophrenia: Identifying Convergent Mechanisms During Development and Moving Toward Prediction

en.block: There is no clear brain mechanism and no biological test.
en.known: It is strongly heritable, involving hundreds of gene variants. A new class of drug acting on muscarinic receptors was approved in 2024.
en.leads: The synaptic pruning hypothesis, very large genetic studies.
en.t: What causes schizophrenia?

sub.en: Can biological markers predict which young people at high risk will actually develop psychosis?
Does cannabis use in adolescence harm the developing human brain the way it does in animal studies?
How can genetic risk scores be made to work as well for people of non-European ancestry?

src.t: Can you predict earthquakes? (USGS)
Machine Learning in Earthquake Seismology
Distributed acoustic sensing for seismic activity monitoring

en.block: No reliable precursor signal has been found.
en.known: We know where the risk is high, but not when a rupture will happen.
en.leads: AI on seismic data, fiber-optic cables used as sensors.
en.t: Can we predict earthquakes?

sub.en: Can the far more detailed earthquake catalogs built by AI reveal new patterns in how earthquakes happen?
Can combining AI with the physics of faults produce earthquake forecasts that are actually useful?
Do signals other than ground shaking, such as chemical or atmospheric changes, carry real warning of an earthquake?

src.t: Why is sleep important? The brain's glymphatic system (University of Rochester)
The new science of sleep: From cells to large-scale societies

en.block: No single function explains why such a risky behavior has been kept everywhere.
en.known: Almost all animals sleep. Sleep helps consolidate memory and clean the brain.
en.leads: Studying sleep in very simple animals, the role of the glymphatic system.
en.t: Why do we sleep?

sub.en: Do rare 'natural short sleepers' really pay no health cost for sleeping much less?
Why do these natural short sleepers seem to need less REM (dreaming) sleep?

src.t: New record lows for battery prices (BloombergNEF)
The design space for long-duration energy storage in decarbonized power systems

en.block: Storage that lasts for days must become much cheaper to replace power plants that run on demand.
en.known: Battery prices have fallen by about 90% since 2010.
en.leads: New technologies designed to store energy for 100 hours or more.
en.t: How can renewable energy be stored cheaply for long periods?

sub.en: Can the cost of storage capacity fall to about 20 dollars per kilowatt-hour, the level needed to cut electricity costs noticeably?
Which technologies could store energy for more than 100 hours both cheaply and efficiently?
Why is it harder for storage to fully replace steady low-carbon power plants in northern regions where more energy uses run on electricity?

src.t: Superconductivity at 250 K in lanthanum hydride under high pressures (Nature, 2019)
Could high-pressure hydrides be high-temperature superconductors? (Physics World)
Clathrate metal superhydrides under high-pressure conditions: enroute to room-temperature superconductivity

en.block: No theory predicts high-temperature superconductors such as the cuprates.
en.known: Some hydrides superconduct near room temperature, but only under extreme pressures.
en.leads: AI-assisted materials discovery, nickelates, automated lab screening.
en.t: Is there a superconductor at room temperature and normal pressure?

sub.en: Can hydride superconductors be made stable at ordinary pressure?
How accurately can theory predict the temperature at which a hydride becomes superconducting?
Can hydrides made of three elements, with a clearly resolved crystal structure, be synthesized and reach higher temperatures?

src.t: On the generalization mystery in deep learning (arXiv)
Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization

en.block: There is no complete theory explaining why, or predicting when it fails.
en.known: Huge networks trained on finite data still work on new examples, contrary to classical statistics.
en.leads: Scaling laws, infinite-width limits, studies of learning dynamics.
en.t: Why do deep neural networks generalize so well?

sub.en: Why do networks that can memorize randomly labelled data still generalize well on real data?
Among all the solutions that fit the training data, how does gradient descent find one that generalizes well?
Can we design a better measure of how much training examples 'agree' with each other (gradient coherence) that takes the network's structure into account?

src.t: Mutual information, islands in black holes and the Page curve (arXiv)
The entropy of Hawking radiation

en.block: If information vanishes with them, a fundamental law of quantum physics is broken.
en.known: Hawking showed that black holes slowly evaporate by emitting radiation.
en.leads: "Islands" and the Page curve, holography, the idea that entanglement and the geometry of space are linked.
en.t: What happens to information that falls into a black hole?

sub.en: Can the exact quantum state of Hawking radiation, not just its entropy, be computed from gravity?
Which geometries, such as 'replica wormholes', must be included in the gravitational calculation, and why?
Should the horizon of an expanding universe also be treated as a quantum system, like a black hole?

src.t: Bekker et al., Twice-yearly lenacapavir or daily F/TAF for HIV prevention in cisgender women (NEJM, 2024)
HIV prevention drug lenacapavir gets FDA approval (NPR, 2025)

en.block: The virus mutates very fast and hides in the body; decades of vaccine trials have failed.
en.known: Treatments make HIV a manageable condition, and long-acting injections can prevent infection.
en.leads: Broadly neutralizing antibodies and mRNA vaccines designed to guide the immune system step by step.
en.t: Can we make a vaccine against HIV?

sub.en: How can a vaccine reliably wake up the rare 'starter' B cells that could grow into makers of broadly neutralizing antibodies?
What do we still need to learn about how B cells develop in order to steer them toward broadly neutralizing antibodies?
How can mRNA vaccines produce HIV's complex outer protein in exactly the right shape?

src.t: NASA's tally of planets outside our solar system reaches 6,000 (NASA, 2025)
NASA records more than 6,000 exoplanets (Scientific American)
Exoplanet Biosignatures: A Review of Remotely Detectable Signs of Life

en.block: No sign of life, or biosignature, has been confirmed beyond Earth.
en.known: More than 6,000 exoplanets are confirmed, many in the zone where water can be liquid.
en.leads: The James Webb telescope, the future Habitable Worlds Observatory, and the Europa Clipper mission to Jupiter's moon Europa.
en.t: Are we alone in the universe?

sub.en: How can we tell oxygen made by life from oxygen made without life (a 'false positive')?
Can planets around small, cool M-dwarf stars be habitable?
What signs could reveal life based on a chemistry different from Earth's?

src.t: Global population to peak this century: World Population Prospects 2024 (IISD)
The Effect of Population Aging on Economic Growth, the Labor Force, and Productivity
9.7 billion on Earth by 2050, but growth rate slowing, says new UN population report

en.block: Fewer workers will support more retirees.
en.known: In 2019 the UN projected that by 2050 about one person in six will be over 65.
en.leads: Healthier aging, automation, migration and pension reform.
en.t: How will aging societies sustain themselves?

sub.en: Can older workers move into industries where automation could make up for missing workers, even though people change jobs less as they age?
Where automation cannot help much, can more immigration and higher work participation make up for an ageing workforce?

src.t: Ocampo et al., In vivo amelioration of age-associated hallmarks by partial reprogramming (Cell, 2016)
Turning back time: Salk scientists reverse signs of aging (Salk Institute, 2016)

en.block: We don't know which cause comes first, or how to rejuvenate without cancer risk.
en.known: We know hallmarks of aging. Partial reprogramming of cells has rejuvenated tissues in mice.
en.leads: Yamanaka factors, senolytic drugs, epigenetic clocks to measure biological age.
en.t: Why do we age, and can it be reversed?

sub.en: Which of the Yamanaka reprogramming factors actually drive the rejuvenation of cells?
Can cells be made younger without losing their identity and without the risk of tumors?
Do epigenetic clocks measure true rejuvenation, or only something that goes along with age?

src.t: International Space Station (NASA)
ISS marks 25 years of continuous human presence in orbit (AIAA, 2025)
Red risks for a journey to the red planet: The highest priority human health risks for a mission to Mars

en.block: Radiation, low gravity and fully closed life-support systems.
en.known: People have lived on the International Space Station continuously since 2000, and reusable rockets have cut launch costs.
en.leads: Lunar bases, using local materials on the Moon and Mars.
en.t: Can humans live permanently beyond Earth?

sub.en: How can astronauts be protected from space radiation, which may raise the risk of cancer, heart disease and memory problems on a trip to Mars?
Why does long spaceflight affect astronauts' eyes and vision, and how can it be prevented?
Can combining a person's genes with all their exposures in space predict how their whole body will respond to a long mission?

src.t: InSAR and its applications to study volcanoes (USGS)
Advances in volcano monitoring driven by the first decade of Sentinel-1 observations
Report Identifies Grand Challenges for Scientific Community to Better Prepare for Volcanic Eruptions

en.block: Many dangerous volcanoes have no monitoring at all.
en.known: Some eruptions have been forecast hours to days ahead from earthquakes, ground swelling and gases.
en.leads: Satellite radar that measures ground deformation, AI on monitoring data.
en.t: Can we forecast volcanic eruptions?

sub.en: Why is it still so hard to forecast large explosive eruptions from ground movements?
Can AI scanning millions of satellite radar images reliably spot volcanoes that are waking up?
What makes the ground at a volcano swell or sink, and when does it mean an eruption is coming?

src.t: The Millennium Prize Problems (Clay Mathematics Institute)

en.block: No one has given it a rigorous mathematical foundation.
en.known: Physicists use this theory of the strong force with great success, and experiments confirm it.
en.leads: Lattice computations, constructive quantum field theory.
en.t: Does Yang–Mills theory have a mass gap?

sub.en: Can quantum Yang–Mills theory be built rigorously in four-dimensional spacetime? No complete example of a quantum gauge theory exists yet.
Why are quarks confined, so that they are never seen on their own?
Does the lattice version of the theory have a proper limit when the lattice spacing shrinks to zero (the continuum limit)?
